paragraphs.text: Air France Flight 447 fell into the Atlantic in a stall.
But that was only the visible part. Air France Flight 447 fell into the Atlantic in a stall. The key figure: 228 ABOARD.

To see why, look at the structure itself. Jun 1, 2009: Pitot icing over the Atlantic; stall. An airliner fell into the Atlantic Ocean. It dropped for minutes in a deep stall, and all two hundred twenty eight aboard died. It began with ice crystals. They blocked the tubes that measure airspeed. The autopilot disconnected, and the crew lost trusted speed data. The nose was held up, and the wings stopped producing lift. The stall was never recognized. Now crews train for high-altitude stalls, and the sensors were replaced.
And the warning signs were already there. The mechanism: pitot tube icing causing autopilot disconnect, followed by a sustained aerodynamic stall.
Then the chain began. The trigger: ice crystals blocking the airspeed sensors. The plane itself was flyable. The airspeed readings came back within about a minute, but the stall had already set in.

This is the moment it could no longer be stopped. Step 1 of the failure chain: ice blocks pitot tubes. Step 2 of the failure chain: airspeed readings drop. Step 3 of the failure chain: autopilot disconnects. Step 4 of the failure chain: nose held up. Step 5 of the failure chain: stall all the way down.
Which leaves one question. What changed: pitot probes were replaced and crews now train on high-altitude stall recovery.
But that was only the visible part. The stall warning went quiet at very low airspeed, then sounded again when the nose lowered. How should a warning behave when data is unreliable?

miniNarrative: The aircraft involved was a four-year-old Airbus A330-203, with serial number 0660, registered as F-GZCP.
It was delivered to the airline in April 2005.
The aircraft underwent a major overhaul on 16 April 2009, and at the time of the accident it had accumulated about 18,870 flying hours.
It was the last Airbus A330 delivered to the airline.
shorts.payoff: At that time, the investigation had established only two facts—the weather near the aircraft's planned route included significant convective cells typical of the equatorial regions, and the speeds measured by the three pitot tubes differed from each other during the last few minutes of the flight.
